Triggers.value: A specific texture associated with the event

Maladaptive Strategies.value: always plan an escape route before entering a place
constantly scan environment for signs of threat
always sit with back against a wall to see the room

Memory.value: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.

issues.item: Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, marked memory gaps alongside very easy verbal access to the trauma is a direct tension. Partial amnesia can coexist with being able to discuss some aspects, but as selected here the items imply opposing states of trauma recall and narrative access, making this node clinically incoherent.

'Incomprehensible chatter' is hard to reconcile with the listed military trauma context when the rest of the profile provides no corresponding memory, threat, or appraisal content involving foreign-language confusion or crowd speech; it reads as a qualitatively different trauma cue from the other triggers.

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' sits in tension with 'Triggered Without Warning' and 'Terror on Recall' at this severity level, because the memory profile otherwise suggests poorly integrated, highly affect-laden trauma recall rather than easy verbal access.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Religious Spaces: Places of worship or religious gatherings
issues.explanation: Avoiding religious spaces is not well supported by the other selected triggers or memory items. There is no religious cue, appraisal, or memory content linking worship settings to the trauma, so this strategy appears clinically disconnected from the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Avoid Authority Figures: Being around people in authority or uniform
issues.explanation: This item appears mis-specified for the node: it describes a trigger/context (being around authority figures or uniforms) rather than a maladaptive strategy/action the patient uses. Within the formulation, Triggers and Maladaptive Strategies are tightly linked, but the selected strategy items should still be coping behaviours. The other strategy items are behaviours (fawning, escape-route planning), whereas this item is a stimulus category, creating within-node incoherence and weakening alignment with the formulation.

For a military trauma profile centered on sensory-triggered re-experiencing, 'Alcohol smell' is not impossible, but it stands out as weakly anchored to the rest of the selected material. The other trigger and memory items suggest combat- or aircraft-related trauma cues and fragmented terror memory; alcohol odor implies a different trauma context unless there is additional explanation. This is not just unusual but clinically hard to integrate with the rest of the profile as presented.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Fawn Response: become overly compliant when feeling threatened
issues.explanation: 'Fawn response' is the least coherent maladaptive strategy given the rest of the profile. The selected triggers and memory items point toward abrupt sensory flashbacks and hypervigilant danger-monitoring, which are well matched by checking surroundings and escape-route planning. Over-compliance as a threat response is more typically associated with interpersonal coercion dynamics and is not well linked to the chosen military/sensory trigger pattern or the active formulation, where Triggers and Maladaptive Strategies are tightly coupled in a vigilance/avoidance loop.

vignette:
Amara's hands, which could trace a suture line with microscopic precision, trembled almost imperceptibly as she recounted the months since her return from deployment. At twenty-five, she was a surgical resident known for her preternatural calm in the operating room, a stark contrast to the coiled tension that now governed her life outside of it. The trauma had occurred nine months prior during her tour as a combat medic. She had been in a field hospital tent when the mortar hit. The first explosion was a deafening concussion that threw her against a wall of sandbags; the second brought the tent down. The memory was not a story she could tell but a series of sensory fragments: the percussive thud of helicopter blades from an incoming medevac, the roar of the blast, and the coarse, gritty texture of the burlap sandbag scraping her cheek as the world dissolved into dust and screaming.

The return to a civilian residency in a busy urban hospital was supposed to be a return to order. For a while, it was. But the memory, fragmented and wordless, began to bleed into the present. Thinking of that day, even trying to suppress the thought of it, seemed to sharpen her senses to a painful degree. The more she replayed the moment of the explosion in her mind, feeling the same gut-wrenching terror she had felt then, the more the city itself seemed to conspire against her. This heightened sensitivity meant that an ordinary day was filled with potential ambushes. The rhythmic chop of a news helicopter overhead was no longer just background noise; it was the sound of incoming wounded, a prelude to chaos that made her heart hammer against her ribs. The sudden bang of a dumpster lid slamming shut in the alley behind the hospital could make her flinch so violently she'd spill her coffee.

In response to this world of latent threats, Amara began to build a fortress of habits. The triggers, whether the roar of a low-flying plane or the rough texture of a canvas laundry cart she brushed against in a corridor, would send a jolt of adrenaline through her, and in its wake, a new rule would form. She started mapping the exits the moment she entered any room-the hospital cafeteria, a lecture hall, even a patient's room. She found herself constantly scanning her surroundings, her eyes sweeping over faces and doorways, searching for anything out of place. In meetings, she would only take a seat against the back wall, a position that felt less exposed, allowing her to keep the entrance in her line of sight. These were not conscious decisions so much as they were deep, instinctual compulsions that promised a sliver of safety in a world that no longer felt safe at all.

This state of constant vigilance, however, began to feed the very anxiety it was meant to quell. Because Amara was always scanning her environment for danger, she became exquisitely attuned to the very sounds and sensations she dreaded. Her focus on threat detection meant she registered every distant siren, every slammed door, every aircraft passing miles overhead-stimuli that her colleagues filtered out as irrelevant city noise. Her hypervigilance ensured she was always the first to notice a potential trigger, which in turn confirmed her belief that the world was an unsafe place requiring constant monitoring. The strategies, meant to protect her, had inadvertently placed her in a feedback loop of her own making, turning her hospital workplace into a minefield of reminders.

The strain was becoming unsustainable. Her colleagues had started to comment on her jumpiness, and her refusal to join them for drinks after a shift-the thought of a loud, crowded bar was unbearable-was creating a social distance she could feel widening. The breaking point came during a pre-op consultation. As she was explaining a procedure to a patient, a construction crew on the street below dropped a sheet of metal, creating a deafening clang. Amara didn't just jump; she dropped into a half-crouch, her hands flying up to cover her head. The patient's look of alarm was more terrifying to her than the noise had been. It was the fear that this "thing," which she couldn't even explain in words, would compromise her ability to be a surgeon-the one part of her identity that still felt whole-that finally brought her to therapy. She was trapped, and she was desperate to find an escape route from her own mind.
